data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is primarily a differential cooling-rate phenomenon driven by the interplay of thermal mass and sky view factor; the cross-city gap is largest where urban materials have high emissivity but the geometry prevents that longwave radiation from escaping to the sky.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If low-emissivity surfaces in dense canyons produce the same nocturnal UHI as high-emissivity surfaces, the emissivity-geometry interaction is not the driver.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the UHI is stronger in open cities with high sky view factor than in dense canyons, the mechanism is falsified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If thermal mass is shown to dominate over emissivity in predicting cooling rates, this mechanism is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Urban surfaces often have high emissivity and would cool efficiently if unobstructed. However, street canyon geometry (low sky view factor) traps the emitted longwave radiation. The nocturnal UHI is therefore strongest where high-emissivity materials are paired with dense building geometry, creating a slow-release heat reservoir that cannot radiatively cool.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
